Assemble It in Word

Build the feature in this order. It runs 900 to 1,200 words; Word shows the count at the bottom of the window.

  1. HeadlineNames the subject in a few words.
  2. StandfirstOne or two sentences that tell a stranger why to read on.
  3. BylineYour name.
  4. LeadHooks a stranger and earns the next paragraph.
  5. Headed sectionsOne idea each, with headings built the same way.
  6. Pull-quoteOne exact line from the novel, with its chapter.
  7. SidebarA short box: a fact, a definition, or a timeline.
  8. Source listAt least two credible sources, one from JStor, in MLA.
  • Every part above is on the page, in this order.
  • Every claim about the novel names its chapter, and every fact about the real world has a source behind it.
  • The file is saved as LastName_FirstName_ThornfieldChronicle_ELA11.docx in Optima, then ELA, then ELA11 in OneDrive.

A

Revise a Model

Read the example, then make three choices.

Example draft
  1. She stays eight years, six as a pupil and then two as a teacher.
  2. That is a long time, and it is many years.
  3. Lowood is a charity school, and Jane is sent there at ten.
  4. The school is bad for the girls in nearly every way.
  5. It also gives Jane a friend and a teacher she admires.

Pass one is the cut. Which sentence helps a stranger most when it goes?

Pass two is the reorder. Which sentence should come first for a reader who has never heard of Lowood?

Pass three is the sharpen. Sentence 4 is vague. Which rewrite would a stranger see most clearly?

B

The Stranger Test

  1. Find someone who has not read the novel.
  2. Hand them only your lead. Ask them to read it and to tell you where they slow down or lose the thread.
  3. Do not explain. Write down where they stalled.
  4. Change that spot, then hand it over again.
What happened Where did your reader stall, and what did you change? 2–4 sentences.
C

One Paragraph, Before and After

Before and after Copy one paragraph from your draft and label it Before. Rewrite it with your cuts, moves and sharper words, and label it After.
A

The Editing Checklist

Revising changes the ideas. Editing fixes the surface. Go through the five points in order.

  • Concision. Cut every word the sentence does not need: “in order to” becomes “to.”
  • Consistent headings and tense. The headings are built the same way, and you write about the novel in one tense throughout.
  • Agreement. Subjects match verbs, and a singular governess stays “she,” not “they.”
  • Quotation punctuation. Every quotation is exact and sits inside quotation marks, with its chapter cited.
  • MLA. Every in-text citation has an entry in the source list, and every entry is cited somewhere in the feature.
B

Punctuating a Quotation

A feature quotes Jane’s refusal in Chapter XXIII and cites it in MLA. Which sentence punctuates the quotation and the citation correctly?

C

Verify Every Quotation

Type each quotation exactly as it will print in your feature, then check it against the novel. The check reports and never changes what you typed.

Pull-quote, as it will print
Exactly as it will appear on the page, without the citation.
Its chapter
For example, XXIII or ch. 23.
Any other quotation Paste any other quotation from your feature to check it. Not counted; use it as often as you like.
D

Verify the Rest

  • Every fact about the real world has a source behind it, or I cut it.
  • Every claim about the novel names its chapter.
  • I opened each source and found the page or passage I cite.
AI and your feature

An AI tool can flag an undefined term or a claim that needs a source. It can also name sources that do not exist, misquote the novel, and state dates and laws with confidence that are wrong. Check every source on JStor and every quotation against the text. Using AI is optional. If you use it, keep a short log of what you asked, what it said, and what you kept, and submit it with your feature.

A

What Changes on a Screen

The Chronicle Online carries the same words. Four things change around them.

Short paragraphsA long block reads as a wall on a screen. Break at each new thought.
Headings as navigationReaders and screen readers jump from heading to heading, so each one has to name its section.
Alt textEvery image carries a sentence that says what is in it, for a reader who cannot see it.
Links to sourcesA source can link to its page, so a reader can check it in one click.
B

Alt Text, Modelled

Model alt text

Drawing: a girl stands very straight before a seated woman in a cap, who raises her hands as if to ward her off.

It says what is in the picture. It does not say what the picture means.

C

Save It as a Web Page

In Word on a computer
  1. Open your finished feature and choose File, then Save As.
  2. In the file type list, pick Web Page.
  3. Name it LastName_FirstName_ChronicleOnline_ELA11.html and save.
  4. Open the saved file in your browser and scroll through it.

Word may also save a folder of supporting files beside the page. Keep the two together. If your Word has no Web Page type, tell your teacher.

Check it on the screen
  • The words match my finished feature.
  • The headline and each heading stand out from the body text.
  • No paragraph is a wall of text.
  • Every image has alt text, and each source is easy to find.
